rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - two-season (2008, 2009) randomized block field experiment on sandy soil in Egypt with surface vs subsurface drip at 100/80/60/40% ETc, three replicates. Q2: Table 2 and Yield and Yield Components - tuber yield measured under drip at each irrigation level; 80% ETc under subsurface drip gave yield comparable to surface drip at full supply (about 38.9-40.4 vs 38.4-40.8 t/ha), authors state 20% water can be saved without affecting yield. Q4: Fig. 1 and Soil Water Distribution - gravimetric soil water content measured at 10-70 cm depth and 5-35 cm radial distance through growth stages; higher root-zone water content (>16% to 40 cm) under subsurface drip linked to higher yield. Q7: Yield and Yield Components - authors state higher yield can be achieved by placing the drip line sufficiently below the soil surface so water reaches the active root zone, and that for drip-irrigated potato on sandy soil subsurface drip is the better option.
rows.notes: Mismatch with passage: the study is on potato (cv. Cara), not tomato, and irrigation levels are fractions of ETc, not of field capacity; the review likely intended a different Badr et al. 2010 tomato paper (listed in this study's references). Rated on what this study shows: yield at 80% ETc was 9.3% lower than full supply overall, but under subsurface drip equal to surface drip at full supply. No non-drip control, so the comparison is between drip variants and water levels. Q3: single method (plot yield). Q8: no limitations stated; soil water data for stressed treatments 'not shown'. Q9: only LSD values in Table 2, no SD/SE/CI.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own two-season field experiment with surface and subsurface drip at four ETc fractions. Q2: Table 3 and Water and Fertilizer Use Efficiency - WUE rose as applied water decreased (e.g. SSD 130-135 at 100% ETc to 212-215 kg/ha/mm at 40% ETc); authors state 20% irrigation water can be saved without affecting potato yield under subsurface drip at 80% ETc. Q4: Fig. 1 and Soil Water Distribution - soil water content measured through the profile; subsurface drip kept water in the root zone, surface stayed dry (about 12%), interpreted as reduced evaporation loss. Q7: Yield and Yield Components / Conclusions - condition stated: drip line placed sufficiently below the surface (15 cm) so water reaches the active root zone and upward capillary flow is restricted; result framed for sandy soil.
rows.notes: Same crop/level mismatch as the previous row: potato not tomato, 80% ETc not 80% field capacity. Water saving is shown as WUE and as equal yield at 80% ETc under subsurface drip; soil evaporation itself was not measured, only inferred from soil water profiles. Q3: single method. Q8: no explicit limitations. Q9: Table 3 reports WUE without any LSD, SD or SE.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - field experiment 2008-2009, SD vs SSD, four irrigation levels, sandy soil, Egypt. Q2: Table 3 and Water and Fertilizer Use Efficiency - at all irrigation levels subsurface drip recorded higher WUE than surface drip (e.g. 212-215 vs 138-155 kg/ha/mm at 40% ETc); Soil Water Distribution - soil water under SSD remained in the root zone and was not lost to deep percolation, surface stayed dry. Q4: Fig. 1 - gravimetric soil moisture mapped by depth and radial distance for both systems at four growth stages; root-zone water content >16% to 40 cm under SSD vs 12% at 40 cm under SD. Q7: Yield and Yield Components / Conclusions - effect depends on placing the drip line sufficiently below the surface within the root level; stated for sandy soil texture.
rows.notes: Supports the WP/water-saving part of the passage (SSD higher WUE, water retained in root zone). Deep seepage and soil evaporation were not measured directly; reduced evaporation and percolation are inferred from the soil moisture contour patterns. Study did not measure weeds. Q3: one method. Q5: single site, soil and crop. Q8: no limitations stated; stressed-treatment soil water data not shown. Q9: WUE in Table 3 reported without dispersion measures.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own two-season field experiment on potato with surface and subsurface drip at four irrigation levels.
rows.notes: The study does not measure weed growth or any pest/weed variable. The only mention of weed control is in the Introduction, citing other work (Enciso et al. 2005; Lamm and Camp 2007; Selim et al. 2009) that a dry soil surface under SSD improves weed control. The study's own results concern soil water distribution (surface dry under SSD), yield, WUE and FUE only.

notes: Full text available including Tables 1-3 and Figs 1-2. Study is a potato field trial comparing surface and subsurface drip at four ETc fractions on sandy soil in Egypt. The LIT_0038 passage describes a tomato result with 80% field capacity, which does not match this paper; a separate Badr et al. 2010 tomato fertigation paper (Healthy Plants 62(1):11-19) is in this study's reference list and is probably the intended citation.
